title: Symmetry Elements and Operations Define the Point Groups
lead: A symmetry operation moves a molecule so that it looks the same afterwards, and each is carried out about a point, a line or a plane. Molecules that share the same set of operations belong to one point group.
summary_html: All molecules can be described in terms of their symmetry or lack thereof, which may contain symmetry elements (point, line, plane). Identity, rotation, reflection, and inversion are symmetry operations (movement of the molecules such that after the movement, all the atoms of the molecules is coincidental with equivalent atom of the molecule in original).
notes: Written by Claire Vallance, Delmar Larsen and Kristin LaRue and shared under the book's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; the renders of Figures 12.2.1 to 12.2.5 from the Symmetry @ Otterbein site of Dean Johnston and coworkers, and the small unlabelled drawings of a molecule beside each point group, are left out, the molecules being drawn in the two figures instead.

figures.original_caption: Figure 12.2.1: Example of Identify Symmetry: The CHFClBr molecule contain no other symmetry other than identity. Figure 12.2.2: Examples of $n$-fold Axis of Rotation: (left) The water molecule contains a $C_2$ axis. (right) Ethane contains both $C_2$ and $C_3$ axes. Figure 12.2.3: Examples of reflection symmetry. (left) The ammonia molecule contains three identical reflection planes. All are designated as vertical symmetry planes ($σ_v$) because they contain the principle rotation axis.(middle) The water molecule contains two different reflection planes. (right) benzene contains a total of seven reflection planes, one horizontal plane ($σ_h$) and six vertical planes ($σ_v$ and $σ_d$). Figure 12.2.4: Examples of Center of Inversion Symmetry. (left) Benzene and (right) staggard ethane have centers of inversion (green balls). Figure 12.2.5: Examples of Improper axis of rotation. (left) Staggered ethane contains an $S_6$ axis of improper rotation. (right) Methane contains three $S_4$ axes of improper rotation. exercises.source_id: the flowchart shown below provides a step-by-step approach to the problem
exercises.prompt: Use the flowchart to find the point group of each molecule: (a) boron trifluoride, BF₃, planar with F–B–F angles of 120°; (b) dichloromethane, CH₂Cl₂; (c) benzene, C₆H₆; (d) chloroform, CHCl₃; (e) trans-1,2-dichloroethene, trans-CHCl=CHCl.

answer.hint: Find the axis of highest order first, then ask whether there are n C₂ axes perpendicular to it.
answer.solution: (a) $D_{3h}$. BF₃ is not linear and has a single $C_3$ axis through B, square to the plane. Three $C_2$ axes lie along the B–F bonds, perpendicular to it, and the molecular plane is a horizontal mirror plane. (b) $C_{2v}$. The only axis is a $C_2$ bisecting both the H–C–H and the Cl–C–Cl angles; there is no $C_2$ perpendicular to it and no horizontal plane, but the H–C–H plane and the Cl–C–Cl plane are two vertical mirror planes. (c) $D_{6h}$. A $C_6$ axis stands square to the ring, six $C_2$ axes lie in the ring and the ring's plane is $\sigma_h$. (d) $C_{3v}$. The $C_3$ axis runs along the C–H bond, there are no perpendicular $C_2$ axes and no $\sigma_h$, and each of the three planes through C, H and one Cl is a vertical mirror plane. (e) $C_{2h}$. The only axis is a $C_2$ square to the molecular plane through the middle of the C=C bond; there are no perpendicular $C_2$ axes, and the molecular plane is a horizontal mirror plane.

exercises.source_id: allowing us to predict whether or not a molecule may be chiral or polar on the basis of its point group
exercises.prompt: BF₃ ($D_{3h}$), CH₂Cl₂ ($C_{2v}$), C₆H₆ ($D_{6h}$), CHCl₃ ($C_{3v}$) and trans-CHCl=CHCl ($C_{2h}$): which of them can have a permanent dipole moment, and which can be chiral?

options: Polar: CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃. Chiral: none.
Polar: CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and trans-CHCl=CHCl. Chiral: none.
Polar: CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃. Chiral: CHCl₃.
Polar: all but benzene. Chiral: trans-CHCl=CHCl.
answer.hint: Only $C_n$, $C_{nv}$ and $C_s$ allow a dipole moment, and a mirror plane or a centre of inversion rules out chirality.
answer.solution: Polar: CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃ only. Their groups, $C_{2v}$ and $C_{3v}$, are $C_{nv}$ groups, so a dipole is allowed along the principal axis. In BF₃ and benzene the $C_2$ axes perpendicular to the principal axis and the $\sigma_h$ plane forbid any dipole. trans-CHCl=CHCl has a centre of inversion, which reverses any dipole, so its two C–Cl bond dipoles cancel. Chiral: none. Every one of the five has at least one mirror plane, and a molecule with a mirror plane is superimposable on its mirror image.

footnotes.html: It is the other way round: molecules that have a centre of inversion are said to be centrosymmetric.

All the operations commute in $C_n$, $S_n$, $C_{nh}$ and $C_{2v}$, but not in $C_{nv}$ for $n \geq 3$: in $C_{3v}$, as Section 12.3 shows, $\sigma_v C_3 = \sigma_v''$ while $C_3 \sigma_v = \sigma_v'$.
